answer:
Let a particle perform uniform circular motion along a circle of radius \(r\) with its centre at \(O\), with constant angular speed \(\omega\). Take \(O\) as the origin, so that the position vector of the particle is \(\overrightarrow{r}\), of constant magnitude \(r\).

The angular velocity \(\overrightarrow{\omega}\) is directed along the axis of rotation, i.e. perpendicular to the plane of the circle, its sense given by the right hand rule.

**Magnitude.** In a small interval \(dt\) the radius vector turns through an angle \(d\theta = \omega\, dt\), and the particle moves along the arc through a distance

\(|d\overrightarrow{r}| = r\, d\theta\)

\(\therefore v = \dfrac{|d\overrightarrow{r}|}{dt} = r\dfrac{d\theta}{dt} = r\omega\)

Since \(\overrightarrow{\omega}\) is perpendicular to \(\overrightarrow{r}\), the magnitude of their cross product is

\(|\overrightarrow{\omega} \times \overrightarrow{r}| = \omega r \sin 90^\circ = \omega r = v\)

so the two magnitudes agree.

**Direction.** The linear velocity \(\overrightarrow{v}\) is along the tangent to the circle at the position of the particle, hence perpendicular to \(\overrightarrow{r}\); it is also perpendicular to \(\overrightarrow{\omega}\), which is along the axis. The vector \(\overrightarrow{\omega} \times \overrightarrow{r}\) is by definition perpendicular to both \(\overrightarrow{\omega}\) and \(\overrightarrow{r}\), and the right hand rule applied to \(\overrightarrow{\omega} \times \overrightarrow{r}\) points it along the tangent in the sense in which the particle is actually moving.

The two vectors therefore have the same magnitude and the same direction.

\(\therefore \overrightarrow{v} = \overrightarrow{\omega} \times \overrightarrow{r}\)

**(D)** \(\dfrac{2vt}{D}\)

The radius of the circle is \(r = \dfrac{D}{2}\).

For uniform circular motion the tangential speed and the angular speed are related by \(v = r\omega\), so

\(\omega = \dfrac{v}{r} = \dfrac{v}{D/2} = \dfrac{2v}{D}\)

The angular speed is constant, so the angular displacement in time \(t\) is

\(\theta = \omega t\)

\(\therefore \theta = \dfrac{2vt}{D}\)

Dimensionally this is a ratio of two lengths, i.e. a pure number, as an angle in radian must be.

In uniform circular motion the tangential acceleration is **zero**.

The tangential acceleration measures the rate of change of the magnitude of the velocity,

\(a_T = \dfrac{dv}{dt}\)

In U.C.M. the particle moves with a constant speed \(v\), so \(\dfrac{dv}{dt} = 0\).

\(\therefore a_T = 0\)

Equivalently, \(a_T = r\alpha\) and the angular speed \(\omega\) is constant in U.C.M., so \(\alpha = \dfrac{d\omega}{dt} = 0\) and \(a_T = 0\).

The particle is still accelerated: the direction of its velocity keeps changing, so it has a radial (centripetal) acceleration of magnitude \(\dfrac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2 r\), directed towards the centre. In U.C.M. the whole of the acceleration is this centripetal part.

The motion of a particle along the circumference of a circle with a **constant speed** is called uniform circular motion (U.C.M.).

Equivalently, the particle covers equal arcs in equal intervals of time, so its angular speed \(\omega = \dfrac{d\theta}{dt}\) is constant and it completes each revolution in the same period \(T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}\).

The **magnitude** of the velocity is constant but its **direction** changes continuously, so U.C.M. is an accelerated motion. The angular acceleration is zero and the acceleration is purely centripetal, of magnitude \(\dfrac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2 r\), directed at every instant towards the centre of the circle.

Consider a particle moving along a circle of radius \(r\). At any instant its linear speed and angular speed are related by

\(v = r\omega\)

The radius of the circular path is constant, so differentiating with respect to time,

\(\dfrac{dv}{dt} = r\dfrac{d\omega}{dt}\)

Here \(\dfrac{dv}{dt} = a\) is the magnitude of the linear (tangential) acceleration and \(\dfrac{d\omega}{dt} = \alpha\) is the magnitude of the angular acceleration.

\(\therefore a = r\alpha\)

In vector form the tangential acceleration is \(\overrightarrow{a_T} = \overrightarrow{\alpha} \times \overrightarrow{r}\), since \(\overrightarrow{\alpha}\) lies along the axis of rotation and is perpendicular to \(\overrightarrow{r}\).

For uniform circular motion \(\alpha = 0\), so \(a = 0\) and only the radial acceleration \(\omega^2 r\) survives.

A particle moving along a circle has a velocity whose direction changes continuously, so even when the speed is constant the particle is accelerated. This acceleration is directed at every instant **towards the centre** of the circle and has magnitude

\(a = \dfrac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2 r\)

By Newton's second law such an acceleration requires a force in the same direction,

\(F = ma = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} = m\omega^2 r\)

**The force acting on a body performing circular motion, directed along the radius towards the centre of the circular path, is called the centripetal force.**

Its features are:

- It is a **real** force. It is not a new kind of force, but is supplied by whatever agency is available in a given situation — the tension in the string for a stone whirled in a circle, the force of static friction for a car on a level road, the horizontal component of the normal reaction on a banked road, the gravitational force for a planet or a satellite, and the electrostatic force of attraction for the electron in Bohr's model of the atom.
- It is always **perpendicular to the velocity** of the body, so it does no work on the body and cannot change its speed. It changes only the direction of the velocity, and so keeps the body on the circular path.
- Without it the body would fly off along the tangent in a straight line, obeying Newton's first law.
- Its magnitude \(\dfrac{mv^2}{r}\) grows with the speed and falls as the radius increases, which is why a sharp turn taken fast is the most difficult one.

| Centripetal force | Centrifugal force |
|---|---|
| It is a **real** force. It arises from an interaction with some other body and has a definite agency — tension, gravitation, friction, normal reaction or electrostatic attraction. | It is a **pseudo** (fictitious) force. It has no agency and arises only because the frame of reference used is an accelerated one. |
| It is observed in an **inertial** frame of reference. | It is experienced only in the **non-inertial** (rotating) frame attached to the revolving body. |
| It is directed along the radius, **towards** the centre of the circular path. | It is directed along the radius, **away** from the centre of the circular path. |
| Its magnitude is \(\dfrac{mv^2}{r} = m\omega^2 r\). | Its magnitude is also \(\dfrac{mv^2}{r} = m\omega^2 r\). |
| It obeys Newton's third law, so a reaction force exists for it. | There is no reaction force for it, as it is not due to any interaction. |
| It is what keeps the body on the circular path; a stone whirled in a circle is held in by the tension in the string. | It is what an observer sharing the circular motion feels as an outward pull; a passenger in a car taking a turn feels pushed outwards. |

The two are therefore **not** an action-reaction pair. They are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, but they are described in two different frames of reference, and only one of them is a real force.

**Data:** \(r = 5\text{ cm} = 0.05\text{ m}\), \(n = 90\text{ r.p.m.} = \dfrac{90}{60} = 1.5\text{ rev/s}\), \(g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2\).

The coin moves in a horizontal circle, so the centripetal force on it must be supplied by the force of static friction between the coin and the turntable. The coin stays in place only while

\(mr\omega^2 \leq \mu_s\, mg\)

It just begins to slip when the friction reaches its limiting value, so at that speed

\(mr\omega^2 = \mu_s\, mg\) \(\therefore \mu_s = \dfrac{r\omega^2}{g}\)

The angular speed is

\(\omega = 2\pi n = 2\pi \times 1.5 = 3\pi = 9.4248\text{ rad/s}\)

\(\omega^2 = 88.83\text{ rad}^2/\text{s}^2\)

\(\therefore \mu_s = \dfrac{0.05 \times 88.83}{9.8} = \dfrac{4.4413}{9.8}\)

\(\therefore \mu_s = 0.4532\)

Check: the largest friction force per unit mass available is \(\mu_s g = 0.4532 \times 9.8 = 4.441\text{ m/s}^2\), and the centripetal acceleration needed by the coin is \(r\omega^2 = 0.05 \times 88.83 = 4.441\text{ m/s}^2\) — the same value, as it must be at the point of slipping.

Only the distance of the coin from the axis enters the result; the radius of the turntable itself plays no part, and neither does the mass of the coin.
twin: Coefficient of static friction between a coin and a gramophone disc is 0.5. Radius of the disc is 8 cm. Initially the centre of the coin is 2 cm away from the centre of the disc. At what minimum frequency will it start slipping from there?

answer:
**Data:** \(r = 400\text{ m}\), \(v = 32\text{ m/s}\), \(g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2\).

The curve is flat (unbanked), so the whole of the centripetal force must be supplied by the force of static friction between the tyres and the road:

\(f_s = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}\)

Static friction cannot exceed its limiting value \(\mu_s N = \mu_s mg\), so the car does not slide only if

\(\dfrac{mv^2}{r} \leq \mu_s\, mg\) \(\therefore \mu_s \geq \dfrac{v^2}{rg}\)

\(\therefore (\mu_s)_{\min} = \dfrac{v^2}{rg} = \dfrac{(32)^2}{400 \times 9.8} = \dfrac{1024}{3920}\)

\(\therefore (\mu_s)_{\min} = 0.2612\)

Check: the maximum safe speed with this coefficient is \(\sqrt{\mu_s rg} = \sqrt{0.2612 \times 400 \times 9.8} = \sqrt{1024} = 32\text{ m/s}\) — exactly the speed given.

Consider a vehicle of mass \(m\) taking a turn of radius \(r\) on a **horizontal** (unbanked) circular track with speed \(v\).

Three forces act on it:

- its weight \(mg\), vertically downwards;
- the normal reaction \(N\) of the road, vertically upwards;
- the force of static friction \(f_s\) between the tyres and the road, horizontal.

There is no vertical acceleration, so

\(N = mg\)

The road is horizontal, so the only horizontal force available is friction. It must therefore supply the entire centripetal force, and it is directed towards the centre of the turn:

\(f_s = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}\)

But static friction has an upper limit,

\(f_s \leq \mu_s N = \mu_s\, mg\)

where \(\mu_s\) is the coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the road. Hence

\(\dfrac{mv^2}{r} \leq \mu_s\, mg\) \(\therefore v^2 \leq \mu_s\, r g\)

\(\therefore v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s\, r g}\)

This is the maximum speed at which the vehicle can safely negotiate the horizontal circular track. Above it the required centripetal force exceeds the largest friction the road can offer and the vehicle skids outwards.

The result is **independent of the mass** of the vehicle, and it depends on the road surface only through \(\mu_s\). Since \(\mu_s\) falls sharply when the road is wet, oily or dusty, the safe speed on such a road is much smaller — which is the reason curved roads are banked instead of being left flat.
twin: Why are curved roads banked?

answer:
**Data:** \(\theta = 10^\circ\), \(v_{\max} = 36\text{ km/hr}\), \(\pi = 3.142\). The value of \(g\) is not stated, so \(g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2\) is used.

\(v = 36 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = 10\text{ m/s}\)

On a banked road the horizontal component of the normal reaction supplies the centripetal force and the vertical component balances the weight:

\(N\sin\theta = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}\), \(N\cos\theta = mg\)

Dividing,

\(\tan\theta = \dfrac{v^2}{rg}\) \(\therefore r = \dfrac{v^2}{g\tan\theta}\)

\(\tan 10^\circ = 0.1763\)

\(\therefore r = \dfrac{(10)^2}{9.8 \times 0.1763} = \dfrac{100}{1.728} = 57.87\text{ m}\)

The length of the circular track is its circumference:

\(L = 2\pi r = 2 \times 3.142 \times 57.87\)

\(\therefore L = 363.7\text{ m}\)

Check: with \(r = 57.87\text{ m}\) the safe speed is \(\sqrt{rg\tan\theta} = \sqrt{57.87 \times 9.8 \times 0.1763} = \sqrt{100} = 10\text{ m/s} = 36\text{ km/hr}\) — the speed given.
twin: Part of a racing track is to be designed for a radius of curvature of 72 m. We are not recommending the vehicles to drive faster than 216 kmph. With what angle should the road be tilted?

answer:
It depends on whether the road is horizontal or banked.

**On a horizontal (unbanked) road — no.** There the centripetal force needed for a turn is supplied entirely by the force of static friction between the tyres and the road, and the maximum safe speed is

\(v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s\, r g}\)

If friction is made zero, \(\mu_s = 0\) and \(v_{\max} = 0\). No horizontal force is then available to bend the path, so by Newton's first law the vehicle would continue in a straight line along the tangent and slide off the curve. It could not even be started or stopped, since the driving force and the braking force are both forces of friction.

**On a banked road — yes, but only at one particular speed.** On a road banked at an angle \(\theta\) the normal reaction \(N\) is not vertical, and its horizontal component can itself provide the centripetal force:

\(N\sin\theta = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}\), \(N\cos\theta = mg\) \(\therefore \tan\theta = \dfrac{v^2}{rg}\)

So a frictionless banked road is perfectly safe at the speed

\(v = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}\)

which is called the optimum or safety speed of that road. At any speed other than this one, friction would be required to make up the difference — an excess of \(N\sin\theta\) has to be balanced at lower speeds and a deficit made up at higher speeds — so on a perfectly frictionless banked road the vehicle can be driven safely only at that single speed.
twin: Why are curved roads banked?

answer:
**Data:** \(r = 200\text{ m}\), \(v = 25\text{ m/s}\). The value of \(g\) is not stated, so \(g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2\) is used.

For a road banked at an angle \(\theta\), with the maximum speed attained without depending on friction,

\(N\sin\theta = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}\), \(N\cos\theta = mg\)

Dividing,

\(\tan\theta = \dfrac{v^2}{rg} = \dfrac{(25)^2}{200 \times 9.8} = \dfrac{625}{1960}\)

\(\tan\theta = 0.3189\)

\(\therefore \theta = \tan^{-1}(0.3189) = 17^\circ 41'\) i.e. \(17.69^\circ\)

Check: \(\sqrt{rg\tan\theta} = \sqrt{200 \times 9.8 \times 0.3189} = \sqrt{625} = 25\text{ m/s}\) — the speed given.

The angle of banking does not depend on the mass of the vehicle, so the same track is safe for a car and for a loaded truck alike.

answer:
The angle of banking \(\theta\) of a road of radius of curvature \(r\), banked for a speed \(v\), is given by

\(\tan\theta = \dfrac{v^2}{rg}\) \(\therefore \theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{v^2}{rg}\right)\)

where \(g\) is the acceleration due to gravity.

At this speed the horizontal component of the normal reaction alone supplies the necessary centripetal force, so no friction is required; \(v = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}\) is therefore called the optimum or safety speed of the road. The angle of banking is independent of the mass of the vehicle.

Consider a body of mass \(m\) tied to a string of length \(r\) and whirled along a vertical circle with centre \(O\). Let \(A\) be the lowest point, \(B\) the midway point where the string is horizontal, and \(C\) the highest point. Let the speeds there be \(v_L\), \(v_M\) and \(v_H\). Take the lowest point \(A\) as the reference level for potential energy.

The heights of the three points above \(A\) are \(0\), \(r\) and \(2r\) respectively, so:

| Position | Height above \(A\) | Kinetic energy | Potential energy | Total energy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lowest point \(A\) | \(0\) | \(\dfrac{1}{2}mv_L^2\) | \(0\) | \(\dfrac{1}{2}mv_L^2\) |
| Midway \(B\) | \(r\) | \(\dfrac{1}{2}mv_M^2\) | \(mgr\) | \(\dfrac{1}{2}mv_M^2 + mgr\) |
| Highest point \(C\) | \(2r\) | \(\dfrac{1}{2}mv_H^2\) | \(2mgr\) | \(\dfrac{1}{2}mv_H^2 + 2mgr\) |

The tension in the string is at every instant along the radius and the velocity is along the tangent, so the tension is always perpendicular to the displacement and does **no work**. Gravity is a conservative force. Hence the total energy is the same at all three positions:

\(\dfrac{1}{2}mv_L^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_M^2 + mgr = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_H^2 + 2mgr\)

**The particular case of the minimum (just-completing) motion.** At the highest point the weight and the tension both point towards the centre:

\(T_H + mg = \dfrac{mv_H^2}{r}\)

A string can only pull, so \(T_H \geq 0\), and the least possible speed at the top is the one for which the string just goes slack, \(T_H = 0\):

\(v_H^2 = gr\)

Substituting in the energy equation, \(v_L^2 = v_H^2 + 4gr = 5gr\) and \(v_M^2 = v_L^2 - 2gr = 3gr\). The energies then become

| Position | Kinetic energy | Potential energy | Total energy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lowest point \(A\) | \(\dfrac{5}{2}mgr\) | \(0\) | \(\dfrac{5}{2}mgr\) |
| Midway \(B\) | \(\dfrac{3}{2}mgr\) | \(mgr\) | \(\dfrac{5}{2}mgr\) |
| Highest point \(C\) | \(\dfrac{1}{2}mgr\) | \(2mgr\) | \(\dfrac{5}{2}mgr\) |

\(\therefore\) the total energy is \(\dfrac{5}{2}mgr\) at every point of the circle, the kinetic energy falling and the potential energy rising by exactly the same amount as the body climbs.
twin: Using the energy conservation, derive the expressions for the minimum speeds at different locations along a vertical circular motion controlled by gravity.

answer:
**Data:** \(m = 50\text{ kg}\), \(r = 3\text{ m}\), \(g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2\).

At the highest point of the vertical circle the weight \(mg\) and the normal reaction \(N\) of the cage both point downwards, i.e. towards the centre, and together they supply the centripetal force:

\(N + mg = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}\) \(\therefore N = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} - mg\)

The cage can only push inwards, so \(N \geq 0\). Contact is just about to be lost when \(N = 0\), and the speed there is the least possible speed:

\(\dfrac{mv_{\min}^2}{r} = mg\) \(\therefore v_{\min} = \sqrt{gr}\)

\(\therefore v_{\min} = \sqrt{9.8 \times 3} = \sqrt{29.4}\)

\(\therefore v_{\min} = 5.42\text{ m/s}\)

The angular speed at the highest point is

\(\omega = \dfrac{v_{\min}}{r} = \dfrac{5.42}{3}\)

\(\therefore \omega = 1.807\text{ rad/s}\)

Check: the centripetal acceleration at this speed is \(r\omega^2 = 3 \times (1.807)^2 = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2 = g\), as it must be when gravity alone provides it.

The mass of the motorcyclist does not enter either answer, since it cancels out of the condition \(N = 0\).

answer:
**(C)** \(3mg\)

Let the string be of length \(r\) and let the speeds at the horizontal (midway) position and at the uppermost position be \(v_M\) and \(v_H\).

**At the horizontal position** the string is along the radius and the weight \(mg\) is vertical, i.e. along the tangent, so the weight has no component along the string. The tension alone supplies the centripetal force:

\(T_M = \dfrac{mv_M^2}{r}\)

**At the uppermost position** both the tension and the weight point downwards, towards the centre:

\(T_H + mg = \dfrac{mv_H^2}{r}\) \(\therefore T_H = \dfrac{mv_H^2}{r} - mg\)

The uppermost point is a height \(r\) above the horizontal position, and only gravity does work, so by conservation of energy

\(\dfrac{1}{2}mv_M^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_H^2 + mgr\) \(\therefore v_M^2 - v_H^2 = 2gr\)

Subtracting the two tensions,

\(T_M - T_H = \dfrac{m}{r}\left(v_M^2 - v_H^2\right) + mg = \dfrac{m(2gr)}{r} + mg = 2mg + mg\)

\(\therefore T_M - T_H = 3mg\)

The difference depends only on the weight of the bob — not on the radius, and not on how fast the bob is being whirled.
twin: Using the energy conservation, derive the expressions for the minimum speeds at different locations along a vertical circular motion controlled by gravity. Also prove that the difference between the extreme tensions depends only upon the weight of the object.

Consider a particle of mass \(m\) tied to a string of length \(r\) and revolving in a vertical circle with centre \(O\). Let \(A\) be the lowest point, \(B\) the midway point where the string is horizontal, and \(C\) the topmost point. Let \(v_L\), \(v_M\) and \(v_H\) be the speeds there.

**Topmost position \(C\).** Both the tension \(T_H\) and the weight \(mg\) are directed downwards, i.e. towards the centre, so together they provide the centripetal force:

\(T_H + mg = \dfrac{mv_H^2}{r}\) \(\therefore T_H = \dfrac{mv_H^2}{r} - mg\)

A string can only pull, never push, so \(T_H \geq 0\). The circle is just completed without the string slackening when \(T_H = 0\):

\(\dfrac{mv_H^2}{r} = mg\)

\(\therefore v_H = \sqrt{gr}\)

**Lowest position \(A\).** The topmost point is a height \(2r\) above the lowest point. The tension is always perpendicular to the velocity and does no work, so the mechanical energy is conserved:

\(\dfrac{1}{2}mv_L^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_H^2 + mg(2r)\) \(\therefore v_L^2 = v_H^2 + 4gr = gr + 4gr = 5gr\)

\(\therefore v_L = \sqrt{5gr}\)

**Mid-way position \(B\).** This point is a height \(r\) above the lowest point, so again by conservation of energy

\(\dfrac{1}{2}mv_M^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_L^2 - mgr\) \(\therefore v_M^2 = 5gr - 2gr = 3gr\)

\(\therefore v_M = \sqrt{3gr}\)

Hence the three minimum speeds are

\(v_L = \sqrt{5gr}\), \(v_M = \sqrt{3gr}\), \(v_H = \sqrt{gr}\), i.e. \(v_L : v_M : v_H = \sqrt{5} : \sqrt{3} : 1\)

Check: \(v_L^2 - v_H^2 = 5gr - gr = 4gr\), which is exactly \(2g(2r)\), the change in speed squared demanded by a fall through the height \(2r\).
twin: Using the energy conservation, derive the expressions for the minimum speeds at different locations along a vertical circular motion controlled by gravity.

**(A)** \(2mgr\)

The potential energy is measured from the lowest point of the vertical circle, which is the usual choice of reference level for this motion.

The highest point of a circle of radius \(r\) lies a height

\(h = 2r\)

above the lowest point. Hence the gravitational potential energy of the particle there is

\(\text{P.E.} = mgh = mg(2r)\)

\(\therefore \text{P.E.} = 2mgr\)

With the same reference level the midway position, where the string is horizontal, is at a height \(r\) and has potential energy \(mgr\).

**Statement.** The moment of inertia of a body about any axis is the sum of its moment of inertia about a parallel axis passing through its centre of mass and the product of the mass of the body with the square of the perpendicular distance between the two axes.

\(I_o = I_c + Mh^2\)

where \(M\) is the mass of the body, \(I_c\) its moment of inertia about the axis through the centre of mass \(C\), and \(h\) the perpendicular distance between the two parallel axes.

**Proof.** Let \(I_o\) be the moment of inertia of the body about an axis through the point \(O\), and \(I_c\) its moment of inertia about a parallel axis through the centre of mass \(C\), the two axes being a distance \(h = OC\) apart.

Consider a mass element \(dm\) of the body situated at the point \(D\). Drop a perpendicular \(DN\) from \(D\) on to the line \(OC\) produced. Then by the definition of moment of inertia,

\(I_o = \int (DO)^2\, dm\) and \(I_c = \int (DC)^2\, dm\)

From the right angled triangle \(DNO\),

\((DO)^2 = (DN)^2 + (NO)^2 = (DN)^2 + (NC + CO)^2\)

\((DO)^2 = (DN)^2 + (NC)^2 + 2(NC)(CO) + (CO)^2\)

But from the right angled triangle \(DNC\), \((DN)^2 + (NC)^2 = (DC)^2\), and \(CO = h\). Hence

\((DO)^2 = (DC)^2 + 2h(NC) + h^2\)

Multiplying by \(dm\) and integrating over the whole body,

\(I_o = \int (DC)^2\, dm + 2h\int (NC)\, dm + h^2\int dm\)

The first integral is \(I_c\) and the last is \(Mh^2\). In the middle term, \(\int (NC)\, dm\) is the algebraic sum of the moments of all the mass elements about an axis through the **centre of mass**, and by the very definition of the centre of mass this sum is zero:

\(\int (NC)\, dm = 0\)

\(\therefore I_o = I_c + Mh^2\)

**Conditions.** The theorem holds for a body of any shape, laminar or three-dimensional, provided the two axes are parallel and one of them passes through the centre of mass of the body.
twin: State the conditions under which the theorems of parallel axes and perpendicular axes are applicable. State the respective mathematical expressions.

answer:
**Definition.** The radius of gyration of a body about a given axis is the distance from that axis at which, if the **entire mass** \(M\) of the body were concentrated as a single point, its moment of inertia would be equal to the actual moment of inertia of the body about that axis.

If \(I\) is the moment of inertia and \(K\) the radius of gyration,

\(I = MK^2\) \(\therefore K = \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{M}}\)

Its SI unit is the metre and its dimensions are \([M^0L^1T^0]\).

**Physical significance.**

- It expresses, as a **single length**, how the mass of the body is distributed about the axis. The larger \(K\) is, the farther the mass lies from the axis, the greater the moment of inertia, and the harder it is to change the rotational state of the body.
- It is **independent of the mass** of the body: for a body of a given shape \(I \propto M\), so \(M\) cancels in \(K = \sqrt{I/M}\). A wooden disc and an iron disc of the same radius have the same radius of gyration. It depends only on the shape and size of the body and on the position and orientation of the axis — a disc has \(K = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}}\) about its central axis but \(K = \dfrac{R}{2}\) about a diameter.
- It does for rotational motion what the centre of mass does for translational motion: it replaces a body of complicated shape by an equivalent point mass, so that the whole mass distribution need not be summed afresh for every problem.
- It makes results compact. The total kinetic energy of a rolling body is \(\dfrac{1}{2}Mv^2\left(1 + \dfrac{K^2}{R^2}\right)\), in which the shape of the body enters only through the single pure number \(\dfrac{K^2}{R^2}\).
twin: Discuss the necessity of radius of gyration. Define it. On what factors does it depend and it does not depend?

answer:
**Data:** radius of gyration about the given axis \(K = 0.5\text{ m}\), distance of that axis from the centre of mass \(h = 0.4\text{ m}\). Let \(K_c\) be the radius of gyration about the parallel axis through the centre of mass.

By the definition of radius of gyration, \(I_o = MK^2\) and \(I_c = MK_c^2\).

By the theorem of parallel axes,

\(I_o = I_c + Mh^2\)

\(MK^2 = MK_c^2 + Mh^2\) \(\therefore K^2 = K_c^2 + h^2\)

\(\therefore K_c^2 = K^2 - h^2 = (0.5)^2 - (0.4)^2 = 0.25 - 0.16 = 0.09\)

\(\therefore K_c = 0.3\text{ m}\)

Check: \((0.3)^2 + (0.4)^2 = 0.09 + 0.16 = 0.25 = (0.5)^2\) — the three lengths satisfy the parallel-axes relation exactly.

**(C)** different linear velocities and same angular velocity

In a rigid body the distance between any two particles is fixed. When such a body rotates about a fixed axis, every particle describes a circle about that axis and turns through the **same angle** in the same interval of time. Hence every particle has the same angular displacement, and therefore the same angular velocity

\(\omega = \dfrac{d\theta}{dt}\)

The linear velocity of a particle at a perpendicular distance \(r\) from the axis is

\(v = r\omega\)

Since \(\omega\) is common to all the particles while \(r\) is different for particles at different distances from the axis, the linear velocities are different — a particle on the axis is at rest, and a particle at the rim moves fastest.

\(\therefore\) all particles have different linear velocities and the same angular velocity.

**Statement.** The moment of inertia of a body about any axis is equal to the sum of its moment of inertia about a parallel axis passing through its centre of mass and the product of the mass of the body with the square of the perpendicular distance between the two axes.

\(I_o = I_c + Mh^2\)

**Proof.** Let \(I_o\) be the moment of inertia of the body about an axis through a point \(O\), and \(I_c\) its moment of inertia about a parallel axis through its centre of mass \(C\). Let the perpendicular distance between the two parallel axes be \(h = OC\).

Consider a mass element \(dm\) at a point \(D\) of the body, and drop a perpendicular \(DN\) from \(D\) on the line \(OC\) produced. By definition,

\(I_o = \int (DO)^2\, dm\), \(I_c = \int (DC)^2\, dm\)

From the right angled triangle \(DNO\),

\((DO)^2 = (DN)^2 + (NO)^2 = (DN)^2 + (NC + CO)^2\)

\((DO)^2 = \left[(DN)^2 + (NC)^2\right] + 2(NC)(CO) + (CO)^2\)

Using \((DN)^2 + (NC)^2 = (DC)^2\) from the right angled triangle \(DNC\), and \(CO = h\),

\((DO)^2 = (DC)^2 + 2h(NC) + h^2\)

Multiplying by \(dm\) and integrating over the whole body,

\(I_o = \int (DC)^2\, dm + 2h \int (NC)\, dm + h^2 \int dm\)

The middle integral is the algebraic sum of the moments of all the mass elements about the centre of mass, and this is zero by the definition of the centre of mass. With \(\int dm = M\),

\(\therefore I_o = I_c + Mh^2\)

**Conditions.** The two axes must be parallel and one of them must pass through the centre of mass; the body may be of any shape, laminar or three-dimensional.

**Application.** For a thin uniform rod of mass \(M\) and length \(L\), \(I_c = \dfrac{ML^2}{12}\) about a transverse axis through its centre. A parallel transverse axis through one end is at \(h = \dfrac{L}{2}\), so

\(I_o = \dfrac{ML^2}{12} + M\left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{ML^2}{12} + \dfrac{ML^2}{4} = \dfrac{ML^2}{3}\)

**Definition.** The moment of inertia of a rotating rigid body about a given axis is the sum of the products of the masses of all the particles of the body and the squares of their respective perpendicular distances from the axis of rotation.

If the body consists of \(N\) particles of masses \(m_1, m_2, \ldots, m_N\) at perpendicular distances \(r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_N\) from the axis, then

\(I = m_1 r_1^2 + m_2 r_2^2 + \cdots + m_N r_N^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{N} m_i r_i^2\)

For a body whose mass is distributed continuously this becomes

\(I = \int r^2\, dm\)

**SI unit:** \(\text{kg m}^2\)

**Dimensions:** \([M^1L^2T^0]\)

Moment of inertia is the rotational analogue of mass: it measures the opposition a body offers to a change in its rotational motion, exactly as mass measures the opposition to a change in translational motion. Unlike mass, however, it is not a fixed property of the body alone — it depends also on the position and orientation of the axis about which the body rotates.

**(B)** \(\dfrac{MR^2}{2}\)

Consider a uniform disc of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\) rotating about its central axis, which passes through its centre and is perpendicular to its plane. Its mass per unit area is

\(\sigma = \dfrac{M}{\pi R^2}\)

Take a thin ring element of radius \(x\) and width \(dx\), concentric with the disc. Its area is \(2\pi x\, dx\), so its mass is

\(dm = \sigma\,(2\pi x\, dx) = \dfrac{M}{\pi R^2}(2\pi x\, dx) = \dfrac{2M}{R^2}x\, dx\)

Every part of this ring is at the same distance \(x\) from the axis, so its moment of inertia is

\(dI = x^2\, dm = \dfrac{2M}{R^2}x^3\, dx\)

Integrating over the whole disc, from \(x = 0\) to \(x = R\),

\(I = \dfrac{2M}{R^2}\int_0^R x^3\, dx = \dfrac{2M}{R^2}\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^R = \dfrac{2M}{R^2}\cdot\dfrac{R^4}{4}\)

\(\therefore I = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2\)

**Definition.** The moment of inertia of a body about a given axis of rotation is the sum of the products of the masses of all the particles of the body and the squares of their respective perpendicular distances from that axis.

For a body made of \(N\) particles of masses \(m_1, m_2, \ldots, m_N\) at perpendicular distances \(r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_N\) from the axis,

\(I = \sum_{i=1}^{N} m_i r_i^2\)

and for a continuous distribution of mass,

\(I = \int r^2\, dm\)

**SI unit:** \(\text{kg m}^2\)

**Dimensions:** \([M^1L^2T^0]\)

It is the rotational analogue of mass, and it appears in the rotational equations exactly where mass appears in the translational ones — \(\tau = I\alpha\) in place of \(F = ma\), \(L = I\omega\) in place of \(p = mv\), and \(\dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2\) in place of \(\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2\).

**(A)** \(0.0625\text{ kg m}^2\)

**Data:** \(M = 0.25\text{ kg}\), \(R = 0.5\text{ m}\).

The ring is thin, and the axis passes through its centre perpendicular to its plane. Every mass element of the ring is therefore at the same perpendicular distance \(R\) from the axis, so

\(I = \sum m_i R^2 = R^2 \sum m_i = MR^2\)

\(\therefore I = 0.25 \times (0.5)^2 = 0.25 \times 0.25\)

\(\therefore I = 0.0625\text{ kg m}^2\)

Check: the radius of gyration is \(K = \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{0.0625}{0.25}} = 0.5\text{ m} = R\), as it must be for a ring about this axis, since the whole of its mass already lies at the distance \(R\).

**(C)** 3 m/s

**Data:** \(I = 5\text{ kg m}^2\), \(\omega = 6\text{ rad/s}\), \(m = 20\text{ kg}\).

The kinetic energy of the rotating body is

\(E_{\text{rot}} = \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times (6)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 36 = 90\text{ J}\)

The translational kinetic energy of the moving mass is \(E_{\text{trans}} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2\). Equating the two,

\(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times v^2 = 90\) \(\therefore 10v^2 = 90\) \(\therefore v^2 = 9\)

\(\therefore v = 3\text{ m/s}\)

Check: \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times (3)^2 = 90\text{ J}\) — the same energy as the rotating body.

**Data:** \(I = 1\text{ kg m}^2\), \(\omega_0 = 30\text{ rad/s}\), \(\omega = 0\), \(t = 10\text{ minutes} = 600\text{ s}\).

The frictional torque is constant on the average, so the angular retardation is uniform:

\(\alpha = \dfrac{\omega - \omega_0}{t} = \dfrac{0 - 30}{600} = -0.05\text{ rad/s}^2\)

The torque on the wheel is given by

\(\tau = I\alpha = 1 \times (-0.05)\)

\(\therefore \tau = -0.05\text{ N m}\)

The negative sign shows that the torque opposes the rotation, which is what a frictional torque must do.

\(\therefore\) the average frictional torque is \(0.05\text{ N m}\), i.e. \(5 \times 10^{-2}\text{ N m}\).

Check by angular momentum: the wheel loses angular momentum \(L = I\omega_0 = 1 \times 30 = 30\text{ kg m}^2/\text{s}\) in 600 s, so the average torque is \(\dfrac{\Delta L}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{30}{600} = 0.05\text{ N m}\) — the same value.

**Data:** \(E = 1000\text{ J}\), \(\omega_1 = 20\text{ rad/s}\), \(\omega_2 = 30\text{ rad/s}\).

The energy spent goes wholly into increasing the rotational kinetic energy of the wheel, so

\(E = \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega_2^2 - \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega_1^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}I\left(\omega_2^2 - \omega_1^2\right)\)

\(\therefore I = \dfrac{2E}{\omega_2^2 - \omega_1^2} = \dfrac{2 \times 1000}{(30)^2 - (20)^2} = \dfrac{2000}{900 - 400} = \dfrac{2000}{500}\)

\(\therefore I = 4\text{ kg m}^2\)

Check: with \(I = 4\text{ kg m}^2\) the kinetic energies are \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 400 = 800\text{ J}\) and \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 900 = 1800\text{ J}\), and their difference is \(1000\text{ J}\) — the energy actually spent.

Consider a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis with a uniform angular speed \(\omega\). Imagine the body to be made up of \(N\) particles of masses \(m_1, m_2, \ldots, m_N\) situated at perpendicular distances \(r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_N\) from the axis of rotation.

Every particle of a rigid body turns through the same angle in the same time, so all of them have the **same angular speed** \(\omega\). The linear speed of the \(i^{\text{th}}\) particle is therefore

\(v_i = r_i\omega\)

and its kinetic energy is

\(E_i = \dfrac{1}{2}m_i v_i^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}m_i r_i^2 \omega^2\)

The total kinetic energy of the body is the sum of the kinetic energies of all its particles:

\(E = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \dfrac{1}{2}m_i r_i^2 \omega^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\omega^2 \sum_{i=1}^{N} m_i r_i^2\)

But \(\sum m_i r_i^2 = I\), the moment of inertia of the body about that axis.

\(\therefore E = \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2\)

Writing \(I = MK^2\), where \(M\) is the mass of the body and \(K\) its radius of gyration, the same result is

\(E = \dfrac{1}{2}MK^2\omega^2\)

This is the rotational analogue of \(\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2\), with the moment of inertia \(I\) replacing the mass \(m\) and the angular speed \(\omega\) replacing the linear speed \(v\).

**Statement.** The angular momentum of a body, or of a system of bodies, remains constant in magnitude as well as in direction if the **net external torque** acting upon it is zero.

**Proof.** For a body of moment of inertia \(I\) rotating about a fixed axis with angular speed \(\omega\), the angular momentum is

\(L = I\omega\)

Differentiating with respect to time,

\(\dfrac{dL}{dt} = I\dfrac{d\omega}{dt} = I\alpha\)

and since \(I\alpha = \tau\), the net external torque,

\(\tau = \dfrac{dL}{dt}\)

Hence, if the net external torque acting on the body vanishes,

\(\tau = 0\) \(\therefore \dfrac{dL}{dt} = 0\)

\(\therefore L = I\omega = \text{constant}\)

so that between any two instants

\(I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2\)

The angular speed of the body therefore increases when its moment of inertia is reduced, and decreases when the moment of inertia is increased.

**Illustration — a diver.** A diver leaves the springboard with the body stretched, so the moment of inertia about the axis of the somersault is large and the rotation is slow. In the air, gravity acts at the centre of mass and exerts no torque about it, so the angular momentum is conserved. On folding the body tightly, \(I\) falls sharply and \(\omega\) rises, allowing several somersaults to be completed in the short time of the fall; the body is stretched out again just before entering the water, which raises \(I\), slows the rotation and gives a clean entry.

The spinning ballet dancer who folds the arms inwards to spin faster is the same effect.

**(D)** \(4\pi\text{ W}\)

**Data:** \(\tau = 2\text{ N m}\), \(\omega = 2\pi\text{ rad/s}\).

When a constant torque \(\tau\) turns a body through a small angle \(d\theta\), the work done is \(dW = \tau\, d\theta\). The power, i.e. the rate of doing this work, is

\(P = \dfrac{dW}{dt} = \tau\dfrac{d\theta}{dt} = \tau\omega\)

\(\therefore P = 2 \times 2\pi\)

\(\therefore P = 4\pi\text{ W} = 12.57\text{ W}\)

This is the rotational analogue of \(P = Fv\) for translational motion.

**Statement.** The angular momentum of a body, or of a system of bodies, remains constant in magnitude as well as in direction if the **net external torque** acting upon it is zero.

**Proof.** The angular momentum of a body rotating about a fixed axis with angular speed \(\omega\) is

\(L = I\omega\)

where \(I\) is its moment of inertia about that axis. Differentiating with respect to time,

\(\dfrac{dL}{dt} = I\dfrac{d\omega}{dt} = I\alpha = \tau\)

where \(\alpha\) is the angular acceleration and \(\tau\) the net external torque. Thus the torque is the rate of change of angular momentum:

\(\tau = \dfrac{dL}{dt}\)

Now if the net external torque acting on the body is zero,

\(\dfrac{dL}{dt} = 0\)

\(\therefore L = I\omega = \text{constant}\), i.e. \(I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2\)

This is the law of conservation of angular momentum. Since \(L = I(2\pi n)\), the frequency of revolution \(n\) is inversely proportional to the moment of inertia whenever \(L\) is conserved.

**Illustration — a person on a rotating stool.** A person holding heavy weights in the outstretched hands is set slowly rotating on a frictionless stool. On folding the arms in, the weights come closer to the axis, the moment of inertia falls, and the person spins noticeably faster; on stretching the arms out again, the rotation slows down. The only external forces are the weight and the normal reaction, both of which act along the vertical axis and exert no torque about it, so \(I\omega\) is conserved throughout.

An acrobat in a circus and a gymnast tumbling in the air use the same effect.

**Data:** \(M = 100\text{ kg}\), \(R = 1.5\text{ m}\), \(\tau = 2000\text{ N m}\), the flywheel starts from rest, number of revolutions \(N = 4\).

The angular displacement in \(4\) revolutions is

\(\theta = 2\pi N = 2\pi \times 4 = 8\pi = 25.13\text{ rad}\)

The torque is constant, so the work done by it in turning the flywheel through an angle \(\theta\) is

\(W = \tau\theta = 2000 \times 8\pi = 16000\pi\)

\(\therefore W = 5.027 \times 10^4\text{ J}\)

Check by the work-energy theorem. The flywheel is a uniform disc rotating about its own axis, so

\(I = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 100 \times (1.5)^2 = 112.5\text{ kg m}^2\)

\(\alpha = \dfrac{\tau}{I} = \dfrac{2000}{112.5} = 17.78\text{ rad/s}^2\)

Starting from rest, \(\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\theta = 0 + 2 \times 17.78 \times 25.13 = 893.6\text{ rad}^2/\text{s}^2\)

Kinetic energy gained \(= \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 112.5 \times 893.6 = 5.027 \times 10^4\text{ J}\) — the same value as the work done.

**(C)** Torque

For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, the torque and the angular acceleration are related by

\(\tau = I\alpha\)

If the angular acceleration is zero, \(\alpha = 0\), then

\(\tau = I \times 0\)

\(\therefore \tau = 0\)

The other three quantities need not vanish. The moment of inertia \(I = \sum m_i r_i^2\) is a positive quantity fixed by the mass distribution of the body about the axis, and so is the radius of gyration \(K = \sqrt{I/M}\); neither can be zero for a real body. The angular momentum is \(L = I\omega\), and a body with zero angular acceleration is simply one turning with a **constant** angular speed, which may well be non-zero — a wheel spinning steadily has \(\alpha = 0\) but a perfectly definite angular momentum.

\(\therefore\) it is the torque that must be zero.

Consider a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis with a constant angular acceleration \(\alpha\). Imagine the body to be made up of \(N\) particles of masses \(m_1, m_2, \ldots, m_N\) at perpendicular distances \(r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_N\) from the axis of rotation.

Every particle of a rigid body has the **same angular acceleration** \(\alpha\), so the tangential (linear) acceleration of the \(i^{\text{th}}\) particle is

\(a_i = r_i\alpha\)

The tangential force required to produce it is

\(f_i = m_i a_i = m_i r_i \alpha\)

This force acts along the tangent, i.e. perpendicular to \(\overrightarrow{r_i}\), so the torque it exerts about the axis is

\(\tau_i = f_i\, r_i \sin 90^\circ = m_i r_i^2 \alpha\)

All these torques are directed along the same line, the axis of rotation, so the total torque acting on the body is their scalar sum:

\(\tau = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \tau_i = \left(m_1 r_1^2 + m_2 r_2^2 + \cdots + m_N r_N^2\right)\alpha = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{N} m_i r_i^2\right)\alpha\)

But \(\sum m_i r_i^2 = I\), the moment of inertia of the body about that axis.

\(\therefore \tau = I\alpha\)

This is the rotational analogue of \(F = ma\).

**SI unit of torque:** \(\text{N m}\) (newton metre).

**Dimensions of torque:** \([M^1L^2T^{-2}]\)

Although \(\text{N m}\) has the same dimensions as the joule, torque is not a form of energy and its unit is never written as the joule.

Consider a rigid body of mass \(M\), radius \(R\) and radius of gyration \(K\), rolling **without slipping** on a horizontal surface, the centre of mass moving with speed \(V\).

Rolling without slipping means that the point of contact is instantaneously at rest, so the distance covered in one revolution is exactly the circumference. Hence the angular speed of the body about its own axis is

\(\omega = \dfrac{V}{R}\)

Such a motion is the sum of two motions: a **translation** of the centre of mass with speed \(V\), and a **rotation** about the axis through the centre of mass with angular speed \(\omega\). The body therefore possesses two kinds of kinetic energy.

**Translational kinetic energy**

\(E_{\text{trans}} = \dfrac{1}{2}MV^2\)

**Rotational kinetic energy.** The moment of inertia about the central axis is \(I = MK^2\), so

\(E_{\text{rot}} = \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(MK^2\right)\left(\dfrac{V}{R}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}MV^2\cdot\dfrac{K^2}{R^2}\)

**Total kinetic energy**

\(E = E_{\text{trans}} + E_{\text{rot}} = \dfrac{1}{2}MV^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}MV^2\dfrac{K^2}{R^2}\)

\(\therefore E = \dfrac{1}{2}MV^2\left[1 + \dfrac{K^2}{R^2}\right]\)

The shape of the body enters only through the pure number \(\dfrac{K^2}{R^2}\), which is \(1\) for a ring, \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) for a disc, \(\dfrac{2}{5}\) for a solid sphere and \(\dfrac{2}{3}\) for a hollow sphere. For a body that slides without rotating, \(K = 0\) and the expression reduces to \(\dfrac{1}{2}MV^2\), as it should.
twin: Discuss the interlink between translational, rotational and total kinetic energies of a rigid object that rolls without slipping.

answer:
**Data:** \(M = 1\text{ kg}\), \(V = 2\text{ m/s}\), the body is a solid sphere rolling on a table.

For a rolling body of radius of gyration \(K\) and radius \(R\), the total kinetic energy is

\(E = \dfrac{1}{2}MV^2\left[1 + \dfrac{K^2}{R^2}\right]\)

For a solid sphere about its diameter, \(I = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2\), and since \(I = MK^2\),

\(\dfrac{K^2}{R^2} = \dfrac{2}{5} = 0.4\)

\(\therefore E = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1 \times (2)^2 \times \left[1 + 0.4\right] = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 1.4\)

\(\therefore E = 2.8\text{ J}\)

Check: the translational part is \(\dfrac{1}{2}MV^2 = 2\text{ J}\) and the rotational part is \(\dfrac{1}{5}MV^2 = 0.8\text{ J}\), so their sum is \(2.8\text{ J}\), and the two stand in the ratio \(2 : 5\), which is the ratio expected for a solid sphere.
